name: g-helper-linux
request:
# ROG HELPER — Smart Installation and Hardware Integration

Repository:
https://github.com/UdayaSri0/g-helper-linux

MISSION
Implement a professional first-run Setup Assistant and safe
hardware-service integration framework for ROG Helper.

The goal is for users to install ROG Helper and access supported
hardware features without manually configuring multiple services
or running the entire graphical application as root.

Act as a coordinated engineering team:
1. Linux packaging and installation engineer
2. Rust and D-Bus backend engineer
3. ASUS hardware/kernel integration engineer
4. Linux security and PolicyKit engineer
5. GTK4/libadwaita UX engineer
6. QA, documentation and release engineer

Use independent agents where supported, and one integration owner
for overlapping changes.

TARGET ENVIRONMENT
- ASUS ROG Strix G16 G615JMR
- Ubuntu 26.10, Linux kernel 7.3.0-10-generic
- Intel CPU and NVIDIA RTX 5060 Laptop GPU
- Existing ROG Helper session daemon and privileged helper
- PolicyKit and system D-Bus available
- asusd and supergfxd not installed
- Native Aura HID already detected
- CPU/GPU/Mid ASUS fan curve interfaces detected

PHASE 1: FULL REPOSITORY AUDIT

Inspect the actual current source, not only older documentation.
Review:
- Rust workspace and providers
- Session daemon
- Privileged helper and high-level APIs
- D-Bus security policies
- PolicyKit actions
- DEB/RPM packaging
- systemd units
- udev rules
- Setup & Access page
- Existing tests and documentation

Document implemented features, missing dependencies,
privilege boundaries and conflicting service ownership.

Do not replace existing working integrations.

PHASE 2: SMART DEPENDENCY DETECTION

Create a typed dependency and capability registry.

Detect:
- Distribution and version
- Kernel and supported ASUS drivers
- Hardware and DMI identity
- asusd/asusctl availability and API compatibility
- Legacy supergfxd availability
- Current power-profile manager
- NVIDIA driver availability
- GPU MUX and dGPU-disable capabilities
- ASUS WMI fan mappings
- Aura HID readiness
- Privileged helper compatibility
- PolicyKit availability

Distinguish:
- Installed and working
- Installed but stopped
- Installed but incompatible
- Missing optional dependency
- Unsupported distribution
- Unsupported hardware
- Authentication required
- Hardware detected but write access unverified

Do not count normal PolicyKit authentication as an installation error.

PHASE 3: FIRST-RUN SETUP ASSISTANT

Implement a modern Setup Assistant within GTK4/libadwaita.

Required screens:
1. Welcome and system detection
2. Core installation status
3. Optional ASUS platform integrations
4. Hardware feature readiness
5. Proposed installation changes
6. Authorisation and execution progress
7. Installation verification
8. Troubleshooting and finish

Required buttons:
- Check System
- View Setup Plan
- Install Supported Components
- Repair ROG Helper Integration
- Recheck Services
- View Installation Log
- Copy Diagnostics

Before installation, display:
- Exact packages and versions
- Trusted package source
- Services to be changed
- Administrative privileges requested
- Potential conflicts
- Reboot requirements
- Expected feature improvements

Allow cancellation where safe.
Never run an installation automatically on page open.

PHASE 4: SAFE INSTALLATION FRAMEWORK

Make DEB installation register all ROG Helper-owned components:
- Application binary and desktop entry
- Session daemon
- Privileged helper
- D-Bus service configuration
- Minimal PolicyKit actions
- Validated udev integration
- Icons and metadata

Use distro-native package dependency management.

Implement optional dependency installation only for verified,
supported distributions with trusted packages.

Prefer native package-manager APIs when appropriate.
If a privileged installer helper is necessary, use a narrowly
scoped, audited, allow-listed implementation.

Do not:
- Give the GUI permanent root permissions
- Use arbitrary shell strings from the UI as root
- Download and execute remote installation scripts
- Automatically add untrusted package repositories
- Blindly run make install from third-party source
- Modify system permissions globally
- Disable existing services without informed approval

If Ubuntu 26.10 has no verified asusctl package source,
show a safe manual setup explanation instead.

Support failed-install recovery and clear error reporting.

PHASE 5: ASUS PLATFORM INTEGRATION

Implement version-aware asusd integration.

Use runtime D-Bus introspection and validated API contracts.

Investigate:
- Platform performance profiles
- Battery charge thresholds
- Fan-curve integration
- Firmware GPU MUX support
- Hardware capability reporting

Preserve existing native battery and Aura fallbacks.

Detect conflicts with other power-profile managers.
Do not modify conflicting services automatically.

Keep legacy supergfxd support optional.
Do not make deprecated supergfxd the default installation.

Investigate Cardwire only as a separate experimental provider.
No automatic GPU-switching installation or hardware transitions.

PHASE 6: FAN CURVE BACKEND

The target exposes:
- asus hwmon device
- asus_custom_fan_curve device
- Both linked to asus-nb-wmi
- CPU, GPU and Mid fan channels
- Eight curve-point interface candidates per channel

Build a capability-gated ASUS WMI provider.

Verify:
- Same canonical hardware device
- Actual driver identity
- Stable channel mapping
- Supported kernel interface semantics
- Valid curve ranges
- Safe thermal limits
- Permission status
- Firmware Auto restoration
- Readback capability

Never assume the presence of pwm files proves writable control.

Implement simulated and mocked tests first.

Hardware writes require:
- Explicit user Apply
- Per-operation PolicyKit authorisation
- Validated device identity
- Validated safe curve
- Backup of previous values
- Readback verification
- Recovery to firmware Auto on failure

Do not execute physical fan-curve changes during automated tests.

PHASE 7: PERMISSION INTEGRATION

Preserve the existing privileged helper.

All privileged hardware operations must:
- Use typed high-level methods
- Validate input values
- Validate targeted hardware
- Check the original caller
- Authorise through PolicyKit
- Return structured success or failure results

No raw hardware paths supplied by the UI.
No unrestricted shell execution.
No blanket authentication on application startup.

PHASE 8: GUI IMPROVEMENTS

Redesign Setup & Access using the existing visual language.

Include:
- Overall installation health
- Core service readiness
- Optional dependency cards
- Supported hardware capability overview
- Clear next actions
- Progress indicators
- Retry and failure recovery
- Compact advanced diagnostics
- Responsive layout and keyboard accessibility

Reduce repeated status information.

Clearly distinguish optional dependencies from failures.

Keep technical paths and diagnostic detail in expandable sections.

PHASE 9: TESTING

Add automated tests for:
- Fresh installation
- Upgrade from previous versions
- Missing optional services
- Unsupported distributions
- Service/API incompatibility
- Package-manager failure
- User cancellation
- PolicyKit denial
- Concurrent installation attempts
- Incorrect fan mapping
- GPU manager conflicts
- Installer input validation
- Root privilege boundary enforcement
- Hardware write methods in mock mode

Run:
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo build --workspace
cargo test --workspace
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings

Also validate packaging and CI workflows.

PHASE 10: DOCUMENTATION AND DELIVERY

Update relevant architecture, permissions, installation,
troubleshooting, GUI, provider and hardware-support documents.

Record precisely which integrations are:
- Fully working
- Available but not physically tested
- Experimental
- Unsupported

Provide:
1. Implementation summary
2. Changed files
3. Security review
4. Installation workflow
5. Before/after feature matrix
6. Test results
7. Manual hardware validation instructions
8. Known limitations
9. Release readiness assessment

Do not change version numbers, tag, publish releases,
push changes, install system services on the host or perform
physical hardware writes without explicit approval.

Prioritise an installable, secure and maintainable solution
over claiming unsupported hardware features.
